newsitem.title: FRANCE: EMU BANDWAGON MAY STEAL SHOW AT WASHINGTON TALKS.
newsitem.headline: EMU BANDWAGON MAY STEAL SHOW AT WASHINGTON TALKS.

text.p: Europe's plans for currency union may steal the limelight at international finance talks in Washington this weekend amid questions about what it will mean for world economic growth and the dollar.
Europe's finance ministers hold talks with the Group of Seven (G7) rich nations this weekend confident their plans for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 are firmly on track.

That makes all the more pressing questions on whether Europe's combined drive to squeeze budget deficits, in the face of persistent mass unemployment, will continue to dampen economic growth, making it the weak link in the world economy.

And, crucially for the Americans, whether pressure for a policy change builds up to the extent that the fledgling monetary union goes for a weaker exchange rate against the dollar to lift growth and get people back to work.

"I am sure the temptation is very real. The core (richer nothern European states) look at the devaluers with a certain amount of jealousy," Banque Internationale de Placement economist Marie Owens-Thomsen said.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters the last time G7 ministers met at a summit in France in June that he had been surprised how much EMU had dominated the talks.

After talks this weekend in Dublin, where EU ministers set out the nuts and bolts of how EMU will work, that focus is likely to intensify both at the G7 and in the corridors of an International Monetary Fund and World Bank meeting next week.

France in particular would like to see a stronger dollar to make Europe's economies more competitive in world markets, although it is unclear how much support it enjoys from Germany, its main partner in driving monetary union forward.

In an interview with the daily La Tribune Desfosses published on Monday, Arthuis said EMU would mean calls for a stronger dollar would be listened to more. "It is indeed one of the reasons for a single currency," he said.

Europe will have two crucial ways of influencing the dollar-euro rate -- in fixing it at the launch of EMU in 1999 and in managing a potentially big surplus of dollar reserves when central banks merge into the future European Central Bank.

The euro is to be exchanged on a one-for-one basis for the ecu -- potentially a weaker currency since it is based on all countries in the European Union, including those whose economies might not be judged healthy enough for early membership of EMU.
Most argue, however, that the one-for-one commitment will mean that the ecu will rise to reflect the stronger economies of core northern European countries likely to join EMU first.

"The key question is what is the political will in Europe to push up the dollar. At the end of the day, the ecu movements will be reflecting the political statements," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
That factor will also determine whether an expected surplus of central bank dollar reserves is used agressively to push the dollar up through intervention on foreign exchange markets.
But for central bankers, seen ruling EMU via the powerful European Central Bank, there seems little risk of a devaluation which could threaten the primary goal of fighting inflation.

For such anti-inflation hawks, the currency stability created by the euro, the liquity of the vast bond market growing around it, and the euro's potential role as a reserve currency, will lead to lower interest rates which will in themselves give a much-needed lift to growth.
They also insist that Europe needs reform to the labour market rather than a devaluation to create jobs.
"Unemployment is a structural problem in Europe," Owens-Thomsen said, adding there was no evidence that devaluation would boost jobs. "The problem in Europe lies elsewhere."

Brossard also argued that despite French calls for a ministerial council to oversee EMU, which so far have received only a lukewarm response, there was little chance of a united political front to promote devaluation.
"Clearly there is not a European will equivalent to the U.S. will to depreciate the dollar against the yen. There is not a government in Europe to deal with the exchange rate," he said.
